variety: Desiree/Cardinal (common Punjab varieties) - storage temperature data from Lady Rosetta variety study
origin_region: Okara, Sahiwal, Kasur, Sialkot, Punjab (major producing districts)
_temp_sensitivity_deprecated: This linear-additive field is no longer used by spoilage_curve.py as of the exponential-formula fix - kept only for reference/history. Use temp_halving_celsius instead.
_temp_halving_note: Derived from Lady Rosetta study data: 126 days shelf life at 5C vs 84 days (dormancy break) at 25C = 1.5x decay-rate increase over 20C, giving a 34.2C halving temperature via k_new = k_base * 2^(deltaT/halving_temp). This is a gentle slope, consistent with potato tolerating ambient heat far better than fruit crops.
_value_note: PLACEHOLDER - needs AMIS Punjab price data (Dataset 3), commodity likely listed as 'Potato'.
_decay_note: decay_constant_k and temp_sensitivity are estimated from the reported day-thresholds (126 days at 5C vs dormancy break at 84 days at 25C), not literal paper values - potato decays far slower than mango/rice-adjacent produce since it is a dormant tuber, hence the much smaller k than mango crops.
source_citation: Abbasi, K.S., Masud, T., Qayyum, A., Khan, S.U., Abbas, S., Jenks, M.A. Storage stability of potato variety Lady Rosetta under comparative temperature regimes. (Pakistani-authored study, PMAS-Arid Agriculture University Rawalpindi). + Khan, M.A. et al., 'Quality Deterioration of Postharvest Fruits and Vegetables in Developing Country Pakistan: A Mini Overview' (2021) - citing Swat district KPK loss survey.

storage_profiles.notes: 5C maintained tuber dormancy up to 126 days - longest storage life of tested temperatures. Trade-off: associated with increased sugar accumulation and poorer chip/processing color (not a concern for fresh-market sale, relevant mainly for processing-bound potatoes).

15C retained lower sugar content and better quality/chip color than 5C storage, but with increased enzymatic browning-related activity (polyphenol oxidase, peroxidase) over time. Good middle-ground for fresh-market (non-processing) potatoes.

Storage life significantly reduced at 25C - dormancy break occurred by day 84, followed by starch degradation and sprouting. Still far longer than fruit crops even at ambient, since potato is a dormant tuber rather than a ripening fruit.

_loss_stats: Pakistan-specific: 10.08% postharvest potato loss reported in storage, and 3.98% in transport, in Swat district, KPK, Pakistan (source above). Lack of storage facilities and inadequate packaging flagged as main causes.

variety: Common Pakistani market varieties (not variety-specific in source study)
origin_region: Punjab and Sindh (major production + import from India/China in off-season)
harvest_season: Year-round with peaks March-May and September-November
_temp_sensitivity_deprecated: This linear-additive field is no longer used by spoilage_curve.py as of the exponential-formula fix - kept only for reference/history. Use temp_halving_celsius instead.
_temp_halving_note: No multi-temperature Pakistani tomato study was found in our research (the Lahore packing-material study only tested one ambient temperature). Uses the standard horticultural Q10=2 convention (decay rate roughly doubles per 10C) as a reasonable literature-backed default - lower confidence than the derived values for mango/potato/rice, flagged honestly rather than presented as equally research-derived.
_value_note: PLACEHOLDER - needs AMIS Punjab price data (Dataset 3), commodity likely listed as 'Tomato'.
_decay_note: decay_constant_k estimated from the 7-10 day ambient shelf-life range reported below - tomato decays faster than potato (dormant tuber) but slower than mango at equivalent ambient heat, consistent with it being a climacteric fruit with moderate respiration rate.
source_citation: Saeed, A.F.U.H., Khan, S.N., Sarwar, A., Tahira, J.J. (2010). Effect of packing materials on storage of tomato. Mycopath 8(2): 85-89. Institute of Plant Pathology, University of the Punjab, Lahore. + Firdous, N. (2021). Post-harvest losses in different fresh produces and vegetables in Pakistan with particular focus on tomatoes. Journal of Horticulture and Postharvest Research 4(1): 71-86.

storage_profiles.notes: Lahore study (room temp, 20C): corrugated cardboard box packing gave the best result of the three tested materials (wooden crate, cardboard box, nylon mesh bag) - 10 days shelf life before mechanical/fungal damage became significant. Open containers and mesh bags showed accelerated decay due to faster fungal sporulation.

Untreated tomato kept in ambient conditions without proper packaging (e.g. loose in gunny bag) lasts only about 7 days before unacceptable decay/weight loss - this is the realistic baseline for most informal Pakistani market handling.

_loss_stats: Pakistan-specific: up to 30% shipment losses reported due to improper packing material and physical damage. Distance-based losses: 7-9% for farm-to-market distances under 50km, rising to 19-27% for distances over 800km. General Pakistani produce context: 30-50% postharvest losses in developing countries (vs <15% in developed countries), attributed heavily to lack of cold chain due to energy/infrastructure constraints (Firdous, 2021).

variety: Samar Bahisht Chaunsa (primary) / Sufaid Chaunsa (secondary variant - see storage_profiles)
_temp_sensitivity_deprecated: This linear-additive field is no longer used by spoilage_curve.py as of the exponential-formula fix - kept only for reference/history. Use temp_halving_celsius instead.
_temp_halving_note: No multi-temperature study exists specifically for Chaunsa (the MAP paper only tested 13C, the Turkish journal paper only tested 11C). Derived instead from the Fajri mango paper (same genus, only multi-temperature Pakistani mango data available) as a cross-variety proxy: ~21 days at 11C vs ~4.5 days at 32C ambient = 4.67x decay-rate increase over 21C, giving a 9.4C halving temperature. This steep (fast-doubling) slope matches mango's known heat sensitivity.
_value_note: PLACEHOLDER - needs AMIS Punjab price data (Dataset 3). AMIS lists Chaunsa generically (does not distinguish Samar Bahisht vs Sufaid), so one price series covers this whole crop_id.
_merge_note: This entry merges two mango varieties (Samar Bahisht Chaunsa and Sufaid Chaunsa) into one crop_id, since AMIS Punjab market data does not distinguish between them. Samar Bahisht is treated as the primary/dominant reference variety; Sufaid Chaunsa's real research data is preserved below as an additional storage_profile rather than being dropped.
source_citation: Ali, Z., Malik, A.U., Khan, A.S., Amin, M., Rehman, A. (2019). Effect of modified atmosphere packaging on the postharvest life and quality of mango cv. Samar Bahisht Chaunsa stored at chilling temperature. Pak. J. Agri. Sci. 56(4): 847-856. + Malik, O.H., Malik, A.U., Khalid, M.S., Amin, M., Khalid, S., Umar, M. (2016). Effect of Modified Atmosphere Packaging on Postharvest Quality of Mango cvs. Sindhri and Sufaid Chaunsa During Storage. Turkish J. Agri. Food Sci. Tech. 4(12): 1104-1111.

storage_profiles.notes: [Samar Bahisht Chaunsa] Best quality at 14 days storage in Biofresh MAP bag (92% marketable fruit). Beyond 21 days quality drops sharply. Ripening at 32C recommended over 24C for better peel colour.
[Samar Bahisht Chaunsa] After 21 days, marketable fruit drops to 38% (day 21), 11% (day 28-35). Not recommended for long shipments.

[Sufaid Chaunsa variant, at 11C] Marketable fruit: 90.5% at 14 days, 83.3% at 21 days, 66.7% at 28 days, 42.9% at 35 days. Sufaid Chaunsa has higher disease incidence than Sindhri - needs careful disease management. Kept separately since temp/RH conditions and decay rate differ from Samar Bahisht Chaunsa above.

_temp_halving_note: Same cross-variety derivation as mango_chaunsa (from the Fajri paper's ambient-vs-cold comparison, the only multi-temperature Pakistani mango data available) - Sindhri has no reason to differ meaningfully from Chaunsa in raw heat sensitivity (both are mango, same genus/physiology), even though Sindhri shows better disease resistance and a more predictable decline curve overall.

storage_profiles.notes: Marketable fruit: 78.6% at 14 days, 71.4% at 21 days, 59.5% at 28 days. Normal cold storage max ~21 days per literature cited in paper. Sindhri showed better storage potential than Sufaid Chaunsa with lower disease incidence.

_temp_halving_note: Directly from IRRI's explicitly stated rule: shelf life halves for every 5C temperature increase. This is the highest-confidence temp_halving_celsius value in the whole dataset since it is stated directly by the source, not derived/estimated by us.
_value_note: Price values carried over from original sample data - verify against AMIS
_temp_sensitivity_note: Derived directly from IRRI rule: shelf life halves for every 5C temp increase, or every 1% moisture content increase. temp_sensitivity = ln(2)/5 = 0.139. This is the strongest real-data parameter in the whole dataset since IRRI states it explicitly (not estimated by us).
source_citation: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank - Postproduction: Storage (Moisture content for safe storage; Guidelines for safe storage). knowledgebank.irri.org/step-by-step-production/postharvest/storage

storage_profiles.notes: Storage period: 'weeks to a few months' per IRRI at this moisture level. Risks: molds, discolouration, respiration loss, insect damage, moisture adsorption. Grain moisture equilibrates with surrounding humid air in open storage (hygroscopic), which is why tropical/humid conditions are especially risky.
IRRI: moisture at 13% or less is required for 8-12 months safe storage. Main risk at this level is insect damage (mold risk drops once below 14%).

IRRI: farmer's seed storage requires 12% or less moisture (loss of germination is the risk beyond this); for storage under 1 year, 9% or less MC is recommended. Airtight containers (IRRI Superbag, Cocoon) keep MC constant at the level it was sealed at, which is why hermetic storage extends life furthest. Bag storage: 40-80kg jute/woven plastic bags. Bulk storage: at farm or commercial collection houses.
